subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Turkish Tea: Çay
description: A short lesson to help you apply Turkish Tea: Çay.

hook.text: Turkey drinks more tea per capita than any country on Earth—over 3 kg per person annually, beating even Britain.

buildup.text: Turkish çay is brewed in a stacked double teapot called a çaydanlık. Water boils below; strong tea steeps above.

discovery.text: It's served in small tulip-shaped glasses with sugar but never milk. The glass shape shows the tea's ruby-red color.

twist.text: Turkey only started growing tea in 1939, replacing coffee. Now the Black Sea coast produces 280,000 tons annually.

climax.text: Çay is served at every meeting, every shop, and every negotiation. Refusing it stops business before it starts.

punchline.text: Red, sweet, tulip-shaped, non-negotiable. Turkey runs on çay.

quiz.question: Which country consumes the most tea per capita?

details.summary: Turkey is one of the world's largest per-capita tea consumers, drinking over 3 kilograms per person annually. Turkish black tea is brewed using a double teapot called a caydanlik, producing a strong concentrate diluted with hot water. Tea is served in small tulip-shaped glasses throughout the day.
details.whyItMatters: Tea replaced coffee as Turkey's national drink in the 20th century. Understanding this shift reveals how economic policy can reshape cultural identity within a generation.
takeaways: Turkey consumes over 3 kilograms of tea per person per year
Brewing uses a double teapot called a caydanlik
Tea is served in distinctive tulip-shaped glasses

faq.question: Why did Turkey switch from coffee to tea?
faq.answer: After the Ottoman Empire collapsed, coffee imports became expensive. In the 1930s, the Turkish government promoted domestic tea cultivation in the Black Sea region as a cheaper alternative. Within decades, tea overtook coffee as the daily drink.

faq.question: How is Turkish tea typically consumed?
faq.answer: Strong black tea is served in small tulip-shaped glasses without milk, often with sugar cubes on the side. Turks drink tea throughout the day, at home, in offices, and in tea gardens. Offering tea is automatic in any social or business setting. Refusing is almost unheard of.
